subtype: Attending a ritual without full belief [Observer]
passage: At the family's ancestor-remembrance meal in Kuala Lumpur, Wanjiru stood with her husband's relatives before a small table of photographs, food and lit incense. She had been raised in a different tradition and did not share the belief that the dead would come to eat. Xin, the eldest aunt, handed her three sticks of incense. Wanjiru took them, bowed her head as the others did and stayed silent, neither pretending nor pulling away. Xin's hands trembled as she set out her late husband's favourite dish. Wanjiru noticed the aunt's lips moving, telling him something quietly. Across the room a teenage cousin studied his phone. Afterwards Xin squeezed Wanjiru's arm without a word.

qa.q: How many sticks of incense did Xin hand to Wanjiru?
qa.a: Xin handed Wanjiru three sticks of incense.

qa.q: What might Wanjiru have been feeling as Wanjiru stood there without sharing the belief?
qa.a: Wanjiru probably felt respectful and a little outside the belief, wanting to take part honestly without pretending.

qa.q: What choice did Wanjiru make that let her join honestly?
qa.a: Wanjiru took the incense, bowed her head as the others did and stayed silent, neither pretending to believe nor pulling away.

qa.q: What might the ritual have meant for Xin as her hands trembled?
qa.a: Xin was probably feeling love and loss for her late husband, and the ritual gave her a way to tell him something quietly.

grounding: An adult attends a family ritual they do not fully share, sees what it means to the elders and takes part with respect and honesty.

subtype: Attending a ritual without full belief [Observer]
passage: The whole family filled the small hall at the community centre for the new baby's blessing. Grandpa Francis, eighty and leaning on a stick, insisted on leading the prayer himself, the baby held in his arms. Kiran, in the second row, wasn't a believer and felt awkward, but stood with head bowed. Around Kiran most of the aunts closed their eyes; two uncles checked their watches; a young cousin whispered a joke and stopped when nobody laughed. When Francis said the baby's name, his voice cracked, and Kiran looked up to see him blinking hard and smiling at the tiny face. Afterwards Kiran didn't pretend to have prayed. “Thank you for doing that, Grandpa,” Kiran said. Francis nodded and handed Kiran a piece of cake.

qa.q: Where was the baby's blessing held?
qa.a: It was held in the small hall at the community centre.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while standing with head bowed?
qa.a: Kiran felt awkward, since Kiran was not a believer, but still wanted to be respectful.

qa.q: What choice did Kiran make at the end, and why does it show honesty?
qa.a: Kiran said, “Thank you for doing that,” without pretending to have prayed, so the thanks were honest and respectful.

qa.q: What might the blessing have meant to Francis when his voice cracked at the baby's name?
qa.a: Francis was probably moved and proud to bless a new member of the family, and leading the prayer himself seemed to matter deeply to him.

grounding: An adult who does not share the family's belief joins a family blessing, sees how much it means to a grandparent and stays respectful and honest.
